job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Diego Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in a master's in telecommunications networks at Santa Rita University, and I rent a room in a student house with three others. My day is lectures or lab in the morning, then I work on my thesis, which is about tracking faults in a mobile network, and in the evening I cook for the house, because I'm the only one who can. I did electrical and computer engineering and finished top of my year, with an internship at a mobile operator's network operations centre and another testing chips. My mother is a nurse and my father used to drive a taxi until his back gave out. I use an AI assistant now and then for debugging, but I never trust it on a first try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I expected. The tools help me find a bug faster, but they don't design a network. I'd tell my housemates the job market is the same as ever, which means tough but fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm comfortable. Networks need people, there's a shortage in my area, and operators keep advertising for junior engineers. My real pressure is at home, because my dad's back means my mother is carrying the household, and I'd like to start earning soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's in June, apply to the operator where I interned and two equipment makers, and send my mother 150 a month once I'm paid. I'd keep the part-time lab assistant job, about 400 a month, until then. I wouldn't change anything about how I work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I know what comes next and who will hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's pressure at home. What does that look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother works nights, and when she's home she's asleep. My dad does the shopping on his good days. I send 100 a month already from my lab job, and I feel guilty it's not more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change your answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the operator froze hiring. Telcos do that when the economy dips, and I've seen it. But that would be the economy, not AI.

say: The tools help me find bugs, but they don't **design a network**.
The job market is the same as ever: **tough but fair**.
think: I'm comfortable, because operators keep hiring **junior engineers** in my area.
My real pressure is **money at home**, with my father unable to work.
do: Apply to the operator where I interned and two **equipment makers**.
Keep the lab job at **400 a month** until June.
Send my mother **150 a month** once I'm paid.
feel: **Calm**, because I know what comes next.
S0.quote: I send 100 a month already from my lab job, and I feel guilty it's not more.
fieldNote: Diego's calm rests on a **local shortage** of network engineers, not on the AI picture.
His strongest feeling is **family duty**, with his father's back and his mother's night shifts.

steps.text: Apply to the mobile operator where I interned and two equipment makers
Keep the lab assistant job until the master's ends in June
Send my mother 150 a month from my first salary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming and we should get ready, but not panic. The network operations centre where I interned was already using software to sort alarms. I'd tell classmates to learn the tools and still learn the basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I see my internship job in that card. The person in the operations centre who watches alarms, writes the tickets and answers the customer calls is exactly what software does. They've already stopped replacing people who leave, and I noticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my thesis toward automated fault diagnosis, so I'm the one who builds the thing. I'd spend 30 minutes a day on the AI tools until I'm good at them. And I'd apply for field engineering roles as well, climbing towers and fixing equipment, because that stays human for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I have options, but I can see which ones are shrinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You noticed colleagues not being replaced. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A man named Stefan (a colleague at the operations centre) retired in spring and no one took his desk. His work got split between the software and two of us, and nobody called it a cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you climb towers for a living?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, yes, for a while. It pays well, I'm not scared of heights, and it's the sort of job a robot needs three more years to do.

say: Get ready but don't panic: learn the **tools** and still learn the basics.
Software already sorts **alarms** in the operations centre.
think: The desk job I interned in, with alarms and tickets, is what **software** does.
Colleagues who leave are **not replaced**, and nobody calls it a cut.
do: Move my thesis toward automated **fault diagnosis**.
Spend **30 minutes a day** learning AI tools.
feel: **Uneasy**, because I can see which options are shrinking.
S1.quote: A man named Stefan (a colleague at the operations centre) retired in spring and no one took his desk.
fieldNote: Diego's evidence comes from his **internship**: quiet attrition, work absorbed by software, nobody calling it a cut.
He is willing to take **field work** if it pays and lasts longer.

steps.text: Redirect my thesis to automated network fault diagnosis
Practise with AI coding tools for 30 minutes a day
Apply for field engineer roles at the operator and tower companies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's scary, and I'd mean it. I'd tell friends to protect their savings and be ready to move. And I'd say governments should do something for families now, because my parents can't wait for a committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the operations centre and the junior network jobs are gone before I finish. I'd be 26 when the robots arrive, with no desk job and a family that needs money. I'd be the one with a degree in a world where degrees are free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the master's and take any engineering job at once, even a field role on a tower crew. I'd send my mother 200 a month, pay nothing on rent beyond essentials and cut my food bill. I'd also ask my aunt in the city whether I could stay in her spare room, because rent is the first thing that breaks me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd hardly sleep for the first month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most about your parents in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's back needs treatment and my mother's nursing job isn't safe either, because AI can do the notes and paperwork. If my job and hers shrink together, we have almost nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your mother that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm taking the first job I find and I'll look after the bills. She'd say 'finish your degree', and I'd tell her the degree isn't the safe thing anymore.

say: It's **scary**, so protect your savings and be ready to move.
Governments should help **families** now, because committees are too slow.
think: The operations centre and **junior network jobs** are gone before I finish.
I'd hold a **degree** in a world where thinking is free.
do: Leave the master's and take **any engineering job** at once.
Ask my aunt in the city about her **spare room**.
feel: **Alarmed**, and I'd hardly sleep for a month.
S2.quote: I'd be the one with a degree in a world where degrees are free.
fieldNote: Diego's alarm is **household-based**: his father cannot work and his mother's nursing paperwork could be automated.
He would give up the **master's** at once, a big step he says plainly.

steps.text: Leave the master's and take any engineering job within a month
Cut my food bill and rent to the essentials
Ask my aunt for her spare room in the city
Send my mother 200 a month from my first pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us do this well. I'd tell friends to build cash and skills now and I'd back any plan that pays people while they retrain. I'd say we need to look after nurses, drivers and everyone who doesn't have a laptop job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be anxious but not alarmed. By 2031 I'd be 29, with a salary and a stable place, and I could help my parents. The robots come in 2034, and my dad's and my mother's work are on that timeline as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job at the operator and put 300 a month towards my parents' costs and 200 into savings. I'd study at night for a certificate in cloud network automation. And I'd keep an eye on field engineering as a fallback, with my aunt's room as a plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but moving. I'd have a direction and that's half the fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three extra years give you, compared with 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paycheque, a record and my parents' care sorted out before the shock. In 2028 I'm unemployed and scared. In 2031 I'm employed and scared. That's a real difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do about your father in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get him the physio he needs while there's still money, and I'd push him to apply for a disability payment. He's proud and won't ask, so I'd have to.

say: Five years lets us do this **well**, with pay while people retrain.
We must look after **nurses**, drivers and everyone without a laptop job.
think: I'd be **anxious** but not alarmed, with a salary and a stable place.
My parents' **work** is on the same timeline as the robots.
do: Take a job at the operator and put **300 a month** towards my parents.
Study at night for a **network automation** certificate.
feel: **Anxious** but moving, because I'd have a direction.
S3.quote: In 2028 I'm unemployed and scared. In 2031 I'm employed and scared. That's a real difference.
fieldNote: Diego measures the extra time as **paycheque and record** before the shock, which shows how his money picture drives his mood.
He plans to push his father toward **disability support**, knowing his father is too proud to ask.

steps.text: Take a network engineer job at the operator
Put 200 a month into savings and 300 towards my parents' costs
Study at night for a network automation certificate
Help my father apply for a disability payment and physio

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to adjust, if governments plan. I'd tell younger people to learn how networks work, because someone has to understand the plumbing. I'd say we should invest in nurses and care workers' training too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy but hopeful. By 2036 I'd be 34, maybe married, with a decade of experience and a father I could finally help properly. I'd still wonder if there'll be a job for my children in 2050.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, get a stable network job and aim to buy a small flat with my partner in six or seven years. I'd put away 300 a month. And I'd keep learning the tools sensibly, one new skill a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A kind of gentle worry that never leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years change about how you treat the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn them properly, one at a time, instead of in a panic. I'd be a careful, boring expert and that's fine with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned children. How does that sit with all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like two children, and I'd want them to grow up with parents who aren't scared of a letter from the bank. That's what I'm really planning for.

say: Ten years is enough if **governments plan**, and young people should learn how networks work.
We should invest in training for **nurses** and care workers too.
think: I'd be uneasy but **hopeful**, with a decade of experience.
I wonder if there will be a job for my **children** in 2050.
do: Finish the master's and get a **stable network job**.
Aim to buy a small **flat** with my partner in six or seven years.
feel: **Mostly fine**, with a gentle worry that never leaves.
S4.quote: I'd like two children, and I'd want them to grow up with parents who aren't scared of a letter from the bank.
fieldNote: Diego's long-term picture is about **children** and a financial cushion, not career status.
Ten years lets him treat the tools as a **slow, careful skill** instead of a rush.

steps.text: Put away 300 a month towards a flat deposit
Plan to buy a small flat with my partner within seven years
Learn one new network automation tool a year
Hold a stable network engineer job for the decade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'd be unemployed with a family that depends on me. What would help is wage support while people retrain, health care for people like my father, and companies being asked to keep hiring graduates for a few years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people think engineering graduates are safe and rich. I'm neither, and I'm carrying my family's hopes in a world that might not need what I know.

headlineQuote: People think engineering graduates are safe and rich. I'm neither, and I'm carrying my family's hopes in a world that might not need what I know.
portrait: Diego is a 24-year-old **telecom engineering** graduate doing a master's. His mother is a nurse and his father can't work.
He uses AI tools sometimes, sits in the political middle and sees his internship's **desk work** as the part software takes.
His fear is household-based: his mother's nursing paperwork and his own **junior job** could go together.
His mood moves from calm to **alarmed** at two years, and he is only uneasy even at ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be jobless while his family depends on him.
whatWouldHelp: **Wage support** during retraining, health care for people like his father, and hiring of graduates.
